newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Sinn Fein urges clarity on N.Ireland arms.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein urges clarity on N.Ireland arms.

text.p: Sinn Fein told Britain, Ireland and the United States on Sunday that it would reject efforts to disarm its IRA guerrilla backers until talks on a Northern Ireland settlement made progress.

Sinn Fein's chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, said in a keynote speech that "decommissioning" -- the surrender of guerrilla weapons -- was "the biggest stumbling block to forward movement" in the Northern Ireland peace process.

He was speaking the day after British Prime Minister Tony Blair and U.S. President Bill Clinton urged the Irish Republican Army to break with violence for good to allow Sinn Fein to join Anglo-Irish peace talks under way in Belfast for the past year.
McGuinness demanded clarification from Britain and Ireland on how the talks would tackle arms surrender, the issue which has brought them to near standstill over the past year.

"Decommissioning has not yet been removed as an obstacle to the negotiations. What is the demand for decommissioning?" McGuinness asked in a speech commemorating Wolfe Tone, an 18th century Irish nationalist.
"It is the demand that the IRA surrender its weapons before talks begin or before they can make progress. Those who make this demand have no interest in making peace," he said.

His remarks appeared directed at Sinn Fein's ideological opposites, Protestant Unionist parties who want the province to remain British and oppose Sinn Fein's goal of ending British rule to reunite the province with the Irish republic.

They placed decommissioning at the heart of international efforts to breathe new life into the peace talks amid mounting tension in Northern Ireland caused by the IRA murder of two police in Lurgan last Monday and Protestant parades.

McGuinness made brief reference to the IRA killings in his speech but said they, the "ongoing campaign" by British troops in Northern Ireland and attacks on pro-British Loyalists and pro-Irish nationalists were all "potent and tragic reminders."
"They are reminders that there are no cessations (truces) currently in place by any of the armed groups," he said.

Sinn Fein demands that the talks cover a withdrawal of Britain's 18,000 troops, the overhaul of the 92 percent Protestant police and the disarming of the IRA's pro-British Loyalist foes at the same time as IRA decommissioning.

The previous British government of Prime Minister John Major and his successor, Tony Blair, back proposals by the chairman of the Belfast talks, former U.S. Senator George Mitchell, to tackle the issue in parallel with political discussions.
"I think it is the only possibility," Mitchell told the BBC on Sunday.

Mitchell's proposal is a compromise between Major's demand that the IRA disarm first to allow Sinn Fein to get to the talks and Sinn Fein's demands that decommissioning be tackled when a new political settlement is reached.

Blair is expected to spell out in detail his government's position on Sinn Fein's entry to the talks on Wednesday based on contacts his government officials had with McGuinness before the Lurgan killings.
McGuinness said Blair's government "appears to be taking up a position and approach which is an advance on the positions adopted by the last British government."
Britain and Ireland banned contact with Sinn Fein after the IRA ended a 17-month ceasefire in February last year but lifted the ban last month to explore peace prospects.
It was renewed after the Lurgan killings. McGuinness said this was a government mistake because peace talks required "face to face discussions."
